docs.creator: Diffusion Science Radio
docs.description: From 2007: ID Card special - Is Big Brother Stalking You? In March 2007 this special edition examined in depth issues of identity and privacy raised by the proposed introduction of a card to identify everyone using Government services. We spoke with Professor Graham Greenleaf of the University of New South Wales and former New South Wales Deputy Privacy Commissioner Anna Johnston, now of the Australian Privacy Foundation. They explore the issue of function creep by which the access card would become a de facto national identity card and the risks that involves. Engineer Aras Vaichas explains the workings of possible smart card technologies, and how they might be made secure. The show featured a real interview conducted by an Anonymous synthetic voice, and a hacked interview which used new questions spliced in by the Anonymous synthetic voice. Hosted by Darren Osbourne, research by Ian Woolf, co-produced by ian Woolf and Charles Willock. You can see the full list of resources here: http://www.diffusionradio.com/2007/03/id_card_is_big_brother_stalkin.html The show was presented by Darren Osborne and produced by Ian Woolf and Charles Willock from the Diffusion Science Radio team at 2SER Sydney. Is it now possible to ensure complete anonymity for both interviewer and interviewee? What steps are required to eliminate all clues to identity? What are the as-yet-undisclosed "commercial benefits" of the card.

docs.creator: Ian Woolf
docs.description: The NSW State Government Parliamentary Secretary for Renewable Energy, Rob Stokes gave a speech at the 10 minute opening of the Sleek Geeks show at Sydney Town Hall by Karl Kruszelniki and Adam Spencer. He described science as scary, dangerous and divisive, even digging into the common Greek root word with "schism", to explain why science divides people. The reverb in the Town Hall makes the sound hard to follow, here's a transcript: "Science IS scary, and science IS Dangerous. The derivation for the word "science comes from an old Greek word from which we get our current word "schism", it means to divide, it means to separate, to distinguish, discern, to know, but taking that idea to divide, to have issues with the capacity of science to divide peoples, I suppose that's where it becomes scary, where it becomes challenging, where it becomes Dangerous." This may be a great example of why lawyers shouldn't give science speeches, nor be in charge of science. I've uploaded the full speech for comparison. You can hear lots of filler and "but", which attempt to soften the essential message you can hear more easily in the quote audio.

docs.description: Professor Paul Ehrlich from Stanford University spoke at the University of New South Wales on 31st October 2011 to give the Jack Beale Lecture on Population and the Environment: In this exciting lecture Professor Ehrlich will focus on four basic points. First that Homo sapiens is a small group animal, genetically and culturally attuned to existing with 50-150 other people, now trying to live in a group of seven billion. Secondly that the planet is vastly overpopulated, possibly as much as four times the long term carrying capacity. Thirdly his belief that one of the most dangerous myths to infect civilisation is that population and economic growth have no limits and that this myth is symbolic of the failure of education systems and the mass media; and finally the idea that incremental change will save us is comforting but dangerous.

docs.description: Luke Overdevest gave this talk at http://www.philorum.org on Wednesday 15th: In the last decade Derivative culture and Piracy has exploded outwards with the advent of the Internet, and copyright law is only just beginning to catch up. I would like to provoke discussion on the moral viewpoints of a variety of groups from extremes to moderate. To this end I will: Define where trademarks, patents, but mainly copyright law is right now in Australia, and by extension what is piracy; Discuss about derivative culture, including remix culture and fan works. eg. Mona Lisa with a Mustache; Also the policies of fair use of copyrighted material; Define Free Material, Copyleft, Open source and other such cultures, which are exploding outwards. eg. docs.description: Are oceans of acid giving our tropical reefs osteoporosis? Dr Ross Hill is a Chancellor's post doctoral research fellow and lecturer in the UTS Function plant biology and climate change cluster, he explained to Ian Woolf his research on the effects of climate change on calcium-using sea life such as coral reefs. Dr Ross Hill is working to collect enough data to accurately predict the impact on coral reefs and other calcifying oraganisms of climate change. To become a researcher in the UTS Function plant biology and climate change cluster, you'd need to enrol in an Undergraduate Environmental biology, marine biology or forensics degree at UTS, do an honours year of your own research, Then a Masters or PhD. For more information go to science.uts.edu.au

Ian Woolf reports on solar powered sea slugs on the sea floor that can make food from sunlight. Monica Sharma updates us on the fate of the spiders in space, and how a brain implant is giving a paralysed man the power of speech, Caitlin Howlett reports on how turtles evolved their shells. docs.description: Han Sun is an engineer from Beijing China , working on his Master's degree UNSW. His research topic is georeference in Augmented reality. Augmented reality is when parts of the virtual world are projected onto your real-world vision, based on your location. You might see a work of art or a person, neither of which are visible to people who aren't looking through an augmented reality headset. The occulus Rift is a virtual reality headset that shows a video screen to each eye to give you immersive 3D views of virtual worlds. Han has modified an Occulus Rift with two cameras to show you the real world with overlays of computer-generated virtual objects, and GPS to tell the system what part of the world you're looking at. He's scanned the University of New South Wales campus with a drone camera, and plans to scan the city of Sydney with a helicopter. Han gave a talk at the Wearables Sydney meetup group. You can hear noises from the pub in the background. Han is new to English, so you may have to listen more carefully.
